big_idea: If you already run a profitable $1M+ business, your first acquisition is paid for by the target's own profit, through commercial debt, seller finance and seller rollover, not by your savings, as long as the deal passes the 1.5x test.
promise: Walk away able to sketch a first acquisition on one page: what you're buying, who sells, how commercial debt, seller finance and seller rollover fund it, and whether it passes the 1.5x repayment test.

hook.line: If your business does a million a year, you don't need a war chest.
hook.script:
If your business does a million a year, you don't need a war chest to buy your next one.
You need a target that already makes money.
And four things I'm about to draw on this board.
A target. Commercial debt. A seller note. And seller rollover.
Most owners think buying a company starts with saving up a pile of cash.
It doesn't.
It starts with finding a business whose own profit can pay for itself.
And there's one test, one number, that tells you in about two minutes whether a deal works or kills you.
Most first-timers never run it.
I'll show you exactly what it is before this video's over.
hook.on_screen: Josh standing at the whiteboard. As he names each of the four items, he draws a box: TARGET, DEBT, SELLER NOTE, ROLLOVER. On 'one number', he writes a large '?' in the corner of the board and circles it (this becomes 1.5x later).

intro.script:
So this is how to buy your first business, without draining your own bank account to do it.
If you own a profitable business doing a million dollars or more, in the US or Australia, and you've never bought a company before, you're in the right place. This is built for you.
If you're pre-revenue, or you're under a million, this isn't your video yet. Go watch the one on whether you're big enough first, then come back.
Who am I to tell you this? I'm Josh Li. I'm co-founder of G&L M&A Advisory, where we help owners buy companies. And I run my own healthcare holding group. So I'm not reading this off a textbook. I live in these deals.
Here's the roadmap.
First, why buying beats building once you're past a million.
Then what you're actually buying, and who's selling.
Then how it's paid for, which is the part everyone gets wrong.
Then the one test every deal has to pass.
Then your first ninety days, and the two mistakes that sink first-timers.
Let's go.

beats.headline: Why Buying Beats Building Past $1M
beats.script:
Let's start with the obvious step most owners skip.
You've already built one business. You know what that took. Years. Hiring the wrong people. Finding customers one at a time. Figuring out pricing the hard way.
Now here's what happens when you want to double.
Most owners do the same thing again. Hire more. Market more. Grind more. And growth comes in at maybe ten, twenty percent a year if things go well.
While most owners do that... the ones building groups do something different.
They buy growth that already exists.
Think about it. Somewhere near you, there's a business doing what yours does, or something right next to it. It already has customers. It already has staff. It already has profit landing in the bank every month.
The owner built it over twenty or thirty years. You can own it in months.
That's the shift. Building is slow and you pay for it with your time. Buying is fast and, done right, the business pays for itself with its own profit.
And you've got an unfair advantage over almost every other buyer out there. You already run a real business. Lenders and sellers can see that. You've made payroll. You know what a P and L looks like when it's healthy and when it's lying.
That's why I keep saying a million is the line. Below it, buying is a stretch. Above it, you're exactly who sellers and lenders want to talk to.
So if buying is the faster path... what exactly are you buying?
slide: $1M+ owners are the buyers lenders want
beats.visual: Whiteboard: two lines on a simple graph. 'BUILD' climbs slowly; 'BUY' steps up sharply. Josh draws, then turns to camera.
beats.transition: So if buying is the faster path, what exactly are you paying for? It's not what most people think.

beats.headline: What You're Really Buying
beats.script:
Most first-timers think they're buying a building, some equipment, a logo.
You're not.
You're buying three things. Cash flow. Customers. And a team.
Cash flow first. That's the profit the business produces after paying everyone, before the owner takes their cut. In the industry you'll hear it called EBITDA or seller's discretionary earnings. Don't get lost in the letters. It's the money the business throws off every year. That number is what decides the price. And, as you'll see in a minute, it's also what pays for the deal.
Second, customers. Relationships that took someone decades to earn. Repeat buyers. Contracts. Referral sources. You don't have to win them. You inherit them.
Third, the team. People who already know how to do the work. The best businesses to buy are the ones where the staff run the day-to-day, and the owner mostly signs off.
Here's the contrast.
The owner who's thinking like a shopper asks, what's it got? Fancy fit-out, nice vans, a good website.
The owner who's thinking like a buyer asks one question. How much does it make, and will that keep happening after the seller walks out the door?
That's the whole game. Predictable profit you can step into.
So now you know what you're buying. The next question is who on earth would sell you a profitable business... and why?
beats.visual: Whiteboard: draw the TARGET box from the hook bigger, split into three: CASH FLOW, CUSTOMERS, TEAM. Underline CASH FLOW twice.
beats.transition: Which raises the question everyone asks: why would anyone sell a business that makes money?

beats.headline: Who Sells, and Why
beats.script:
Here's the question I get more than any other. Josh, if the business is profitable, why would they sell it?
Because profit isn't the only thing an owner cares about.
Picture the typical seller. They started the business decades ago. They're tired. Maybe their health is telling them to slow down. And the big one: there's nobody to hand it to. The kids don't want it. The managers can't afford to buy it.
So they've got two options. Close the doors and walk away with a few pieces of equipment. Or find a buyer who'll look after the staff and customers they spent their life building.
That's you.
And here's the part first-timers miss. Most of these owners aren't looking for the highest price from a stranger. They want someone they trust to keep it alive. Someone who already runs a real business. Someone who can show them the plan.
While most buyers show up waving a number... the ones who get the deal show up with a plan for the people.
This is also why so many sellers are open to helping fund the sale themselves. They want it to work. They'd rather be paid over time by someone credible than not be paid at all.
Which brings us to the part that decides whether you need a war chest or not.
How does it actually get paid for?
slide: They sell to who they trust
beats.visual: Talking head, tight shot, then cut to whiteboard: write SELLER with three bullets: tired, no successor, wants legacy protected.
beats.transition: And because sellers want it to work, they'll often help pay for it. Here's how the money actually stacks up.

beats.headline: Debt, Seller Finance, Seller Rollover
beats.script:
Quick note before I draw this. I'm going to talk about structure. This isn't legal, tax or financial advice. Every deal and every country is different, so get your own advisers on it.
Now. Back to the four boxes from the start.
You've got the target. Underneath it, three layers of funding.
Layer one, commercial debt. A lender funds a big chunk of the price, and it's repaid out of the business's profit. In the US and Australia the lenders and programs differ, but the logic is the same. They lend against cash flow.
Layer two, seller finance. The seller agrees to be paid part of the price over time, through a note. They become, in effect, a second lender. That tells the bank the seller believes in the business.
Layer three, seller rollover. The seller keeps a slice of equity in the business after the sale. So they're still a part-owner. They stay invested in it going well, and that slice is a piece of the price you don't have to fund with cash on day one.
Stack those three, and the gap left for your own money can get very small. Sometimes close to nothing, depending on the lender and the deal.
While most owners think buying means writing a giant cheque... the ones building groups let the debt, the seller note and the rollover carry the weight, and let the business's profit pay it back.
But there's a catch. None of this works unless the deal passes one test.
beats.visual: Whiteboard: stack three boxes under TARGET: DEBT, SELLER NOTE, ROLLOVER. Shade the tiny remaining gap and label it 'YOUR CASH'. Lower-third disclaimer during first sentence.
beats.transition: Remember the question mark from the start? This is where we fill it in.

beats.headline: The 1.5x Test Every Deal Passes
beats.script:
Here's the number. Remember that question mark? It's one point five.
The test is simple. Take the business's yearly profit. Divide it by the yearly repayments on the debt and the seller note. You want that answer at about one point five or better.
Let's use illustrative numbers. These are made up to show the maths, not a real client deal.
Say the business makes five hundred thousand a year in profit. The price is two million, which is four times profit.
Commercial debt funds one point two million. Seller finance, five hundred thousand. Seller rollover covers the last three hundred thousand. Little or none of it is your cash.
Now the repayments. Illustratively, the debt costs around one eighty a year. The seller note around one fifteen. Call it roughly three hundred thousand a year in repayments.
Five hundred of profit, divided by three hundred of repayments. About one point six seven.
It passes.
Why one point five? Because businesses have bad months. A key staff member leaves. A big customer goes quiet. That buffer is what lets you survive a rough patch and still pay everyone.
While most first-timers fall in love with a business and then try to make the numbers work... the ones who last run this test first, and walk away fast when it fails.
So the deal passes. You sign. Now what happens on Monday morning?
beats.visual: Whiteboard: replace the '?' with 1.5x. Write the illustrative deal in a box clearly titled 'ILLUSTRATIVE NUMBERS'. Persistent on-screen label 'Illustrative example, not a real deal' for the whole beat.
beats.transition: Passing the test gets you the keys. What you do in the next ninety days decides whether it stays a good deal.

beats.headline: Your First 90 Days
beats.script:
Here's where first-timers either lock in the deal, or quietly break it.
The first ninety days have one job. Keep the profit you paid for.
That's it. Not growth. Not your big new ideas. Protect what's there.
Month one: people. Sit down with every key staff member. Tell them what's changing, which should be almost nothing, and what isn't. Uncertainty is what makes good people leave.
Month one, also: customers. The seller introduces you to the biggest ones personally. This is where that rollover pays off again. A seller who still owns a slice wants that handover to go well.
Month two: the numbers. Get weekly visibility on cash, sales and the repayments. You already know how to read a business. Now you're reading two.
Month three: one or two easy wins. Things your current business already does better. Purchasing. Systems. Shared admin. Small, safe improvements.
While most first-time buyers walk in on day one and start changing everything... the ones building groups walk in and change almost nothing until they understand what they bought.
That's not exciting. It's how you keep the cash flow that's paying for the deal.
And that brings me to the two mistakes I see first-timers make again and again. Either one can wipe out everything we've just drawn.
beats.visual: Whiteboard: a simple 90-day timeline split into three columns: M1 PEOPLE + CUSTOMERS, M2 NUMBERS, M3 EASY WINS.
beats.transition: Two mistakes undo all of this. The second one is the one almost nobody sees coming.

beats.headline: The Two First-Timer Mistakes
beats.script:
Mistake number one. Buying the story instead of the profit.
The seller says next year's going to be huge. There's a big contract coming. The growth is just around the corner.
Lovely. You don't pay for next year. You pay for the profit that's already there, proven in the books. If the deal only passes the one point five test using the seller's forecast, it doesn't pass.
Mistake number two. Funding it the hard way.
This is the one nobody sees coming. A first-timer finds a good business, gets excited, and tries to fund it with a bank loan and their own savings. No seller note. No rollover.
Now they've drained their cash. The seller has no reason to help after settlement because they've been paid in full and gone. And if anything wobbles in the first year, there's no buffer.
Compare that to the structure we drew. Commercial debt, seller finance and seller rollover. The seller is still invested. Your own cash is mostly still in your pocket. The repayments are covered one and a half times.
Same business. Two completely different levels of risk.
While most first-timers think the risk is in the business they pick... a lot of the risk is actually in how they pay for it.
So let's bring this all the way back to where we started.
slide: Mistake 2: funding it the hard way
beats.visual: Whiteboard: two big Xs. Under X1 'FORECAST'. Under X2 draw a tall 'YOUR SAVINGS' bar next to the slim 'YOUR CASH' gap from beat 4.
beats.transition: Which brings us right back to the promise from the first ten seconds.

close.script:
So, back to where we started.
You don't need a war chest to buy your first business.
You need a target that already makes money. Commercial debt. Seller finance. Seller rollover. And a deal that clears one point five.
And think about what that gets you.
On the surface, it's a second business. But really, it's a second stream of profit you didn't have to build from scratch.
It's a group, not a job. A team running two businesses, not you running one.
And underneath that, it's the feeling of finally being on the other side of the table. Not grinding for the next ten percent. Owning things that pay you.
That's who the owners building groups become. Buyers. Not just operators.
Now here's the cost of doing nothing.
The sellers you'd want are retiring right now. Every year you wait, the good ones go to someone else. Another year of growing ten percent the slow way. Another year of your profit sitting there when it could be the reason a lender says yes.
You've already done the hard part. You built a business that does a million plus.
If you want help doing the next part properly, apply through the first link in the description. Tell us about your business and what you want to buy. If it's a fit, we'll book a strategy call and look at your first deal together.
